title: Spring Boot — Mock Interview
description: Comprehensive interview test covering the full Spring Boot study notes: setup, profiles, JPA, validation, transactions and locking, Spring Security & JWT, exception handling, testing, file/CSV/PDF, async/scheduling, caching, logging, REST clients, Criteria API, microservices (Eureka, Gateway, Feign, Circuit Breaker, Config), Kafka, Spring Batch, Docker, Liquibase.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Spring Initializr (start.spring.io)?
options: To deploy Spring Boot apps to the cloud
To generate a ready-to-use Spring Boot project structure with selected dependencies and build tool
To run unit tests in the cloud
To replace Maven with a custom build tool
questions.explanation: Spring Initializr scaffolds a project (Maven or Gradle) with the chosen Java version, packaging and starters, ready to import into the IDE.

questions.question: What is a 'starter' dependency such as `spring-boot-starter-web`?
options: A runtime agent that profiles the JVM
A curated set of compatible dependencies grouped behind a single artifact, triggering relevant auto-configuration
A code generator that writes controllers automatically
questions.explanation: Starters bundle a coherent set of versioned dependencies and signal Spring Boot to auto-configure the related features (e.g. `starter-web` brings in Spring MVC + embedded Tomcat + Jackson).

questions.question: Which file is the canonical YAML alternative to `application.properties`?
questions.explanation: Spring Boot reads either `application.properties` or `application.yml` (YAML format) from the classpath.

questions.question: Explain how Spring Profiles work and how you would activate the 'dev' profile.
questions.modelAnswer: Profiles let you group beans and configuration that should only be active in a given environment (dev, test, prod...). You annotate beans or @Configuration classes with @Profile("dev") so they are loaded only when that profile is active. Environment-specific properties go in `application-dev.yml`, `application-prod.yml`, etc. To activate, set `spring.profiles.active=dev` in `application.properties`, pass `--spring.profiles.active=dev` on the command line, or set the env var `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev`. Multiple profiles can be combined.

questions.question: What does `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (included in `@SpringBootApplication`) do?
options: It scans the database and generates entities
It auto-configures Spring beans based on the libraries present on the classpath
questions.explanation: Auto-Configuration inspects classpath, beans and properties, then registers sensible default beans (datasource, MVC, Jackson, JPA, security, ...) which you can still override.

questions.question: Where do you typically declare a custom `PasswordEncoder` bean?
options: Inside a @Configuration class using a @Bean-annotated method
questions.explanation: Custom beans are declared with `@Bean` in a `@Configuration` class so Spring can manage them: `@Bean public PasswordEncoder encoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }`.

questions.question: `spring-boot-devtools` is automatically excluded from production JARs.
questions.explanation: DevTools is intended for development (auto-restart, LiveReload). It is disabled when running a fully packaged app and is not included in the repackaged executable JAR.

questions.question: Which annotation marks a Java class as a JPA entity mapped to a table?
questions.explanation: `@Entity` (with `@Id` for the primary key) maps the class to a database table managed by JPA / Hibernate.

questions.question: Which JPA annotations describe entity relationships?
questions.explanation: @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne and @ManyToMany describe associations (often combined with @JoinColumn / @JoinTable). @RestController is a web stereotype, not a JPA relationship.

questions.question: Which strategy delegates primary-key generation to the database (typically AUTO_INCREMENT)?
questions.explanation: `GenerationType.IDENTITY` relies on the database's auto-increment column. `SEQUENCE` uses a DB sequence; `TABLE` simulates a sequence in a table; `AUTO` lets the provider choose.

questions.question: What does `@Valid @RequestBody UserDTO dto` on a controller method trigger?
options: It serialises the DTO to JSON
It validates the DTO against its constraint annotations (@NotNull, @Size, @Email...) and rejects the request if any fails
It enables CSRF protection on the endpoint
questions.explanation: `@Valid` triggers Bean Validation. If any constraint fails, Spring throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (HTTP 400) — unless a `BindingResult` parameter is present to handle errors manually.

questions.question: Which constraint annotation validates that a String matches an email format?
questions.explanation: `@Email` (Jakarta Bean Validation) validates the email format. `@Pattern(regexp=...)` works too but requires a custom regex.

questions.question: What is `BindingResult` and why must it appear immediately after the @Valid parameter?
questions.modelAnswer: `BindingResult` is the container Spring populates with binding/validation errors when @Valid runs. Declared as the very next parameter after the validated object, it tells Spring NOT to throw `MethodArgumentNotValidException` and to let your controller decide how to react (custom error message, partial save, return 400 with field-level details, etc.). Useful methods: hasErrors(), getFieldErrors(), getAllErrors(). If the position is wrong, Spring won't know which target it refers to.

questions.question: Which Spring MVC annotations route HTTP requests to a controller method?
questions.explanation: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping and the generic @RequestMapping all bind HTTP routes. @Transactional governs transactions, not routing.

questions.question: Which annotation extracts a value from the URI like `/users/{id}`?
questions.explanation: `@PathVariable` binds path segments. `@RequestParam` reads query string parameters; `@RequestBody` binds the JSON body; `@RequestHeader` binds an HTTP header.

questions.question: Extending `JpaRepository<User, Long>` automatically gives you findAll, findById, save, delete and many more methods without writing any code.
questions.explanation: JpaRepository inherits CrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository, providing CRUD, paging, sorting and flushing methods out of the box.

questions.question: What is the role of `@Query` on a Spring Data repository method?
options: It defines a custom JPQL or native SQL query, optionally with @Param-bound parameters
It marks a query as cached
questions.explanation: `@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email")` defines an explicit JPQL (or `nativeQuery=true` for SQL). Parameters are bound by name with `@Param`.

questions.question: By default, when does Spring rollback a `@Transactional` method?
options: Only on RuntimeException or Error (unchecked exceptions)
On any return value other than null
Never — you must call entityManager.rollback() manually
questions.explanation: Default rollback is on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException + Error). To rollback on a checked exception use `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)`.

questions.question: Which propagation always SUSPENDS the existing transaction and starts a brand new one?
questions.explanation: REQUIRES_NEW always starts a new physical transaction, suspending any existing one. Useful for audit/logging that must commit independently.

questions.question: Marking a transaction `readOnly = true` is just a hint and never affects performance.
questions.explanation: It is more than a hint: it lets the JDBC driver/JPA provider skip dirty-checking and flush, can enable read-only JDBC connections / replicas, and signals intent to other developers.

questions.question: Compare optimistic and pessimistic locking in JPA. When would you choose each?
questions.modelAnswer: Optimistic locking adds a `@Version` field that is auto-incremented on update. Two transactions can read the same row concurrently; whichever commits second sees a version mismatch and throws `OptimisticLockException` — the application typically retries. Best for low-contention scenarios; no DB lock is held. Pessimistic locking acquires a real database lock with `LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_READ/WRITE` (e.g. `entityManager.find(Order.class, id, PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)`). Other transactions are blocked or fail until the lock is released. Best for high-contention or short critical sections where conflicts are very likely. Trade-off: optimistic = better throughput, occasional retries; pessimistic = guaranteed exclusivity but more blocking and risk of deadlock.
keyPoints: Pessimistic for high contention / financial ops

questions.question: Which annotation activates Spring Security configuration for an application?
questions.explanation: `@EnableWebSecurity` (combined with a `SecurityFilterChain` bean or `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` in older versions) wires Spring Security into the application.

questions.question: Which interface do you implement to load a user from your database for Spring Security?
questions.explanation: `UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(username)` returns a `UserDetails`. Spring Security calls it during authentication.

questions.question: Which password encoder is recommended by Spring Security today?
questions.explanation: `BCryptPasswordEncoder` (or Argon2/PBKDF2) — strong, salted, slow on purpose. MD5/SHA-1 are insecure for passwords; NoOpPasswordEncoder is for tests only.

questions.question: Which annotations enforce role/permission checks at the method level?
questions.explanation: @PreAuthorize (SpEL, full expressions), @Secured (simple roles) and @RolesAllowed (JSR-250) all enforce method-level authorization. @RequestMapping is for routing.

questions.question: Describe a typical JWT authentication flow in a Spring Boot REST API.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Client POSTs credentials to `/login`. 2) Server authenticates via AuthenticationManager + UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder. 3) On success, server builds a signed JWT (header.payload.signature) containing the username and authorities, e.g. `Jwts.builder().setSubject(...).signWith(HS256, secret).compact()`, and returns it. 4) Client stores the token (Authorization: Bearer header is preferred) and sends it on every subsequent request. 5) A custom filter (`JwtAuthenticationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter`) intercepts each request, extracts the token from the Authorization header, validates the signature and expiration, loads the UserDetails, builds an `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken` and stores it in the SecurityContextHolder. 6) The request reaches the controller fully authenticated. The filter is registered with `http.addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)`. Stateless — no session.

questions.question: Why extend `OncePerRequestFilter` for a JWT filter?
options: It guarantees the filter logic runs at most once per HTTP request, even with internal forwards/dispatches
questions.explanation: OncePerRequestFilter ensures the filter is executed only once per request, avoiding double processing on internal dispatcher forwards — exactly what JWT validation needs.

questions.question: Where should a JWT preferably be stored on the client for a REST API?
options: In the Authorization HTTP header as `Bearer <token>` (or in a HttpOnly + Secure cookie)
In plain localStorage with no protection
Inside a hidden form field on every page
questions.explanation: The standard is `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` for REST APIs. HttpOnly + Secure cookies are also acceptable. Plain localStorage is vulnerable to XSS.

questions.question: What is `@RestControllerAdvice` used for?
options: Centralising exception handling and response shaping across all controllers via @ExceptionHandler methods
questions.explanation: `@RestControllerAdvice` (= @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody) lets you define global @ExceptionHandler methods that translate exceptions into structured JSON error responses for every controller.

questions.question: How do you build a clean error response for a custom 'ResourceNotFoundException'?
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Create the exception (`class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException`) and optionally annotate it with `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)`. 2) Define a DTO `ErrorResponse(timestamp, status, error, message, path)`. 3) In a `@RestControllerAdvice` class, declare `@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)` that builds the DTO and returns `ResponseEntity.status(404).body(dto)`. 4) Optionally add a generic `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` returning 500 to avoid leaking stack traces. Always use a consistent JSON shape so the client can parse errors uniformly.

questions.question: Which Mockito annotation injects mocks into the class being tested?
questions.explanation: `@Mock` creates a mock of a dependency. `@InjectMocks` instantiates the class under test and injects all the @Mock fields into it (constructor, setter or field injection).

questions.question: Which annotation runs a method BEFORE every test in JUnit 5?
questions.explanation: JUnit 5 uses `@BeforeEach` (per test) and `@BeforeAll` (once for the class). The legacy `@Before` belongs to JUnit 4.

questions.question: Which annotation loads the FULL Spring application context for an integration test?
questions.explanation: `@SpringBootTest` boots the entire context. Slice tests like `@WebMvcTest` (controllers only) and `@DataJpaTest` (JPA layer + H2) are faster but more focused.

questions.question: What does `MockMvc` allow you to do?
options: Simulate HTTP requests against your controllers without starting a real server
questions.explanation: MockMvc dispatches requests through Spring MVC infrastructure in-memory: `mockMvc.perform(get("/users/1")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value(...))`.

questions.question: How do you receive an uploaded file in a Spring controller?
questions.explanation: Use `@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file` for a `multipart/form-data` upload, then `file.getOriginalFilename()`, `file.getInputStream()`, etc.

questions.question: Which library is commonly used in Spring Boot to generate Excel files (.xls / .xlsx)?
questions.explanation: Apache POI handles Excel via XSSFWorkbook (xlsx) and HSSFWorkbook (xls). iText is for PDF, OpenCSV for CSV.

questions.question: Which library is the de-facto standard for generating PDF in Java/Spring Boot?
questions.explanation: iText (or its open-source fork OpenPDF) builds PDFs programmatically with `Document`, `Paragraph`, `PdfWriter`, tables and images.

questions.question: Which annotation pair enables asynchronous method execution in Spring?
options: @EnableAsync on a config class + @Async on the method
questions.explanation: `@EnableAsync` activates async support; `@Async` marks methods to run in a separate thread (returning void or a `CompletableFuture`).

questions.question: `@Async` works on methods called from within the same class via `this.method()`.
questions.explanation: Like @Transactional, @Async relies on a Spring proxy. A self-invocation (`this.foo()`) bypasses the proxy, so the call runs synchronously. Inject the bean or split into a separate component.

questions.question: Which expression triggers `@Scheduled` to run every weekday at 8 AM?
questions.explanation: `@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 8 * * MON-FRI")` executes at 08:00 from Monday to Friday. Don't forget `@EnableScheduling`.

questions.question: What does `@Cacheable("products")` do on a service method?
options: Stores the method's return value in the named cache, keyed by the method arguments — subsequent calls with the same args skip the body and return the cached value
Caches HTTP responses on the client side
Forces re-execution of the method on every call
questions.explanation: `@Cacheable` caches results by argument key. `@CacheEvict` removes entries; `@CachePut` always executes the method but updates the cache. Activate with `@EnableCaching` and a CacheManager (Caffeine, EHCache, Redis).

questions.question: What is the ELK stack and why is it used with microservices?
questions.modelAnswer: ELK = Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana (often plus Beats/Filebeat). Logstash (or Filebeat) collects and ships logs from each microservice. Elasticsearch indexes them for fast search and aggregation. Kibana provides dashboards, queries and alerting on top. With many distributed services, you cannot tail individual log files — ELK gives you a centralised, searchable, correlated view (typically with a correlation/trace id propagated across calls) which is essential for debugging and observability.

questions.question: What is a microservices architecture, in one sentence?
options: A monolithic app split into modules but deployed together
A style where the application is composed of small, independently deployable services that communicate over the network, each owning its data
A frontend pattern based on web components
A serverless replacement for Spring Boot
questions.explanation: Microservices = small, independently deployable services with their own data store, communicating via REST/messaging.

questions.question: What is Eureka in the Spring Cloud / Netflix OSS ecosystem?
options: A Service Discovery / registry where microservices register themselves and discover each other
questions.explanation: Eureka Server is a service registry. Each service registers on startup; clients query Eureka to locate instances dynamically, with health checks and auto-deregistration.

questions.question: What is the role of Spring Cloud Gateway?
options: It is an API Gateway that centralises routing, filters, security, rate limiting and request transformation for all microservices
questions.explanation: Spring Cloud Gateway is the modern API Gateway: a single entry point that handles routing, predicates, filters (auth, logging, rewriting), CORS, rate limiting, etc.

questions.question: Compared to RestTemplate, Feign Client is...
options: A declarative HTTP client: you define an interface annotated with @FeignClient and Spring generates the implementation
questions.explanation: Feign is declarative — you describe the API as a Java interface with @FeignClient + @GetMapping etc., and Spring builds the proxy. It also integrates with load balancing and circuit breakers.

questions.question: Which library is the modern, recommended replacement for Hystrix as a circuit breaker?
questions.explanation: Hystrix is in maintenance mode. Resilience4j is the lightweight, modular, modern circuit breaker library used with Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker.

questions.question: Explain the three states of a Circuit Breaker and why this pattern matters.
questions.modelAnswer: States: CLOSED — calls go through normally; failures are counted. OPEN — once a failure threshold is exceeded, calls fail fast (or use a fallback) without contacting the remote service for a 'wait duration'. HALF-OPEN — after the wait, a few trial calls are allowed; if they succeed the breaker returns to CLOSED, otherwise it reopens. Why it matters: in a distributed system a slow or failing dependency can saturate threads and cascade the failure across the whole platform. The breaker isolates the fault, frees resources, lets the dependency recover, and gives the user a graceful fallback.
keyPoints: Auto recovery via half-open trial calls

questions.question: What is the role of Spring Cloud Config Server?
options: It centralises configuration (e.g. on Git) so every microservice fetches its application.yml from one source — supporting refresh without redeploy
questions.explanation: Config Server externalises and centralises configuration (often Git-backed). Combined with `@RefreshScope` and Spring Cloud Bus, beans can be refreshed without redeploying.

questions.question: Which broker is most often used for Event-Driven asynchronous communication between Spring Boot microservices?
questions.explanation: Kafka and RabbitMQ are the dominant choices. Kafka excels at high-throughput, partitioned, persisted event streams; RabbitMQ at flexible routing and traditional queues.

questions.question: In Kafka, what is a 'topic'?
options: A logical channel of messages, divided into partitions for parallelism and ordering
questions.explanation: A topic is a named logical channel. It is split into partitions: each partition is an ordered, append-only log; consumers in the same group share partitions for parallel processing.

questions.question: Which Spring annotation marks a method as a Kafka message consumer?
questions.explanation: `@KafkaListener(topics = "my-topic", groupId = "...")` registers the method to receive messages from the given topic.

questions.question: Describe the standard Reader → Processor → Writer model in Spring Batch.
questions.modelAnswer: A Spring Batch Job is composed of one or more Steps. The classic chunk-oriented Step has three components executed in a loop, transactionally per chunk: ItemReader reads one item at a time from a source (database via JdbcPagingItemReader, file via FlatFileItemReader, JSON, JPA...). ItemProcessor (optional) transforms or filters each item (returning null skips it). ItemWriter writes a whole chunk at once to its destination (DB, file, queue). The Step is configured with `.<I,O>chunk(N)` so every N items form a transactional batch — commit on success, rollback on failure. Batch keeps execution metadata (status, restart points, skip/retry counts) in its own JobRepository, allowing restart, restart-from-failure and idempotent reruns.

questions.question: Which Spring annotation activates Spring Batch?
questions.explanation: `@EnableBatchProcessing` (often on a @Configuration class) wires up the Job/Step builders, the JobRepository and the JobLauncher.

questions.question: What is JPA's Criteria API best suited for?
options: Type-safe DYNAMIC query construction — building WHERE clauses programmatically based on optional filters
questions.explanation: Criteria API (CriteriaBuilder, CriteriaQuery, Root, Predicate) builds queries programmatically. It shines for dynamic search forms where filters are optional and you don't want to concatenate JPQL strings.

questions.question: Which client is the modern, non-blocking, reactive alternative to RestTemplate?
questions.explanation: WebClient returns `Mono`/`Flux` and is non-blocking. RestTemplate is now in maintenance mode; WebClient is recommended even in MVC apps for outbound calls.

questions.question: Common ways to version a REST API include:
questions.explanation: URI, header and query-parameter versioning are all valid. URI is the most common because it is explicit and cache-friendly.

questions.question: Which line in a Dockerfile sets the JVM as the entry point of a Spring Boot image?
questions.explanation: `ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"]` is the canonical way. `EXPOSE` only documents the port, `RUN` executes at build time, `CMD` provides default args.

questions.question: What does Liquibase do in a Spring Boot project?
options: Versions and applies database schema changes via a changelog (XML/YAML/SQL), automatically at startup
questions.explanation: Liquibase tracks schema changes in a changelog of changeSets (with id and author). On startup Spring Boot runs pending changeSets, keeping every environment's DB in a known, repeatable state.

questions.question: List the typical layers of a clean Spring Boot CRUD application and the responsibility of each.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Entity / Model (@Entity) — domain objects mapped to DB tables. 2) Repository (interface extending JpaRepository) — pure data access, no business logic. 3) DTO — data transfer objects exposed to / received from the outside world; decouple the API from the entities. 4) Mapper (manual or MapStruct) — convert between DTO and Entity. 5) Service (@Service) — business logic, validation, orchestration, transactions (@Transactional). 6) Controller (@RestController) — HTTP layer: routing, request/response serialisation, status codes; delegates work to the Service. 7) Exception handler (@RestControllerAdvice) — uniform error responses. 8) Configuration / Security — @Configuration beans, SecurityFilterChain, etc. This separation enforces single responsibility, testability and easy evolution.

questions.question: Spring's `@Transactional` requires the method to be public when using the default (proxy) mode.
questions.explanation: Spring's proxy-based transactions only intercept public methods. Non-public methods are silently ignored unless you switch to AspectJ weaving.

questions.question: Which Spring Boot annotation combines @Configuration, @ComponentScan and @EnableAutoConfiguration?
questions.explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` is the meta-annotation placed on the main class. It includes @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan.

questions.question: Which dependency provides Swagger / OpenAPI documentation in modern Spring Boot 3 applications?
questions.explanation: Springfox is unmaintained and incompatible with Spring Boot 3. The current standard is `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui`, which exposes `/swagger-ui.html` and `/v3/api-docs`.

questions.question: What does the @LoadBalanced annotation on a RestTemplate bean do in Spring Cloud?
options: It enables caching of HTTP responses
It activates client-side load balancing: requests to a registered service name are dispatched to one of the available instances discovered (e.g. via Eureka)
questions.explanation: @LoadBalanced wraps the RestTemplate (or WebClient.Builder) so URLs like `http://user-service/...` are resolved through the discovery client and balanced across instances by Spring Cloud LoadBalancer.

questions.question: What are the main advantages AND drawbacks of a microservices architecture?
questions.modelAnswer: Advantages: independent scalability per service; isolated, faster deployments; technology heterogeneity (each team picks its stack); resilience (failure of one service shouldn't take down the system if circuit breakers and bulkheads are in place); clear domain boundaries; teams can work autonomously. Drawbacks: significant operational complexity (Docker/K8s, observability, CI/CD per service); distributed transactions and eventual consistency are hard; debugging across services requires correlation ids and centralised logging (ELK) + distributed tracing (Zipkin / Sleuth / OpenTelemetry); network overhead and serialisation costs; security must be enforced everywhere (gateway + JWT + service-to-service auth). Microservices pay off only when the domain and the team size justify the overhead — start with a well-modularised monolith if not.
